Title: [Bug]: HAL_DMA_Abort may fail with timeout on certain optimization levels

Body:
### Bug Summary

HAL_DMA_Abort may fail on DMA_SxCR_EN at the H7 (at least M4 Core) on certain GCC optimization levels

### Detailed Description

Dear ST support,

I found an interesting but hard-to-track bug in the HAL_DMA_Abort function which seems to be bus timing related:

The function HAL_DMA_Abort fails (in my code) on the check if the DMA is effectively disabled monitoring the DMA_SxCR_EN register. This happens on the DMA2 + M4 core in the H745 dual core but the M7 core might be affected as well. When it fails it returns a HAL_ERROR (ErrorCode = HAL_DMA_ERROR_TIMEOUT, State = HAL_DMA_STATE_ERROR).

But this fails only on the following (GCC) optimization levels:
-  -O2, -O3, -Ofast, -Os, -Oz
It does not fail on the following optimization levels:
- -O0, -O1, -Og

4. Restart the DMA in multibuffer configuration

Regarding the issue, and in line with the supported HAL flow implemented in **HAL_ADCEx_MultiModeStop_DMA()**, the ADC multimode conversion is stopped first, the driver waits until both master and slave ADC conversions are no longer ongoing, and only then is the DMA aborted.

In your workaround, **HAL_DMA_Abort()** is called immediately after HAL_ADCEx_MultiModeStart_DMA(), while the ADC multimode path is still active. This is not the supported stop sequence and can lead to timing-sensitive behavior, which is consistent with the optimization dependency you observed.

That said, if the single NOP inside HAL_DMA_Abort() works well for your application, you may of course continue to use it as part of your solution. Otherwise, you can submit a post on our [Community](https://community.st.com/) forum for further support.

Title: [Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`

Body:
### Bug Summary

When USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER is **not set** (no 1.8V voltage transceiver), HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation() can still apply ClockDiv = 0 (clock bypass) for cards that report CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED capability. This results in the SDMMC peripheral running at full kernel clock speed (e.g., 100 MHz) on a **3.3V bus**, far exceeding the SD specification limit of 50 MHz for High Speed mode at 3.3V.

### Detailed Description

## Affected Function

[HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation() in Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1723)

## Root Cause

There is an inconsistency between HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation() and HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation():

### ConfigSpeedBusOperation — correctly guarded

metadata.issue_title: [Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`

text:
[HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation()](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1866) uses [#if (USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER != 0U)](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1878) to separate UHS and non-UHS code paths. When there is **no transceiver**, the [SDMMC_SPEED_MODE_AUTO case](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1985) correctly limits the card to **SDR25 (High Speed, 50 MHz)** — it does **not** attempt UHS voltage switching.

### ConfigWideBusOperation — NOT guarded (the bug)

[HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1723) has **no** USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER check. It decides the clock divider based solely on hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed:

metadata.issue_title: [Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`
[Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`

text:
3. **HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()** reads hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed == CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED and applies Init.ClockDiv = hsd->Init.ClockDiv = 0 → **bypass mode (100 MHz on 3.3V bus)**.

## Impact

- The SDMMC bus runs at **100 MHz on 3.3V signaling**, exceeding the SD specification maximum of **50 MHz for High Speed** and **25 MHz for Default Speed** at 3.3V.
- This violates the SD Physical Layer Specification and may cause **data corruption**, **CRC errors**, or **card damage** on some cards.
- It happens to work on some embedded SD NAND chips (e.g., ZBIT, MKFD) that tolerate overclocking on short BGA traces, masking the bug.
- The issue is particularly insidious because the speed negotiation in ConfigSpeedBusOperation is correct — only the clock divider in ConfigWideBusOperation is wrong.

## Reproduction

metadata.issue_title: [Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`

text:
1. Use any STM32H7 board **without** a 1.8V voltage transceiver (USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0).
2. Insert an SD card that reports UHS-I capability (common in SDHC/SDXC cards and embedded SD NAND).
3. Initialize with hsd->Init.ClockDiv = 0 (auto-decide).
4. Call HAL_SD_Init(), then HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation(SDMMC_SPEED_MODE_AUTO), then HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation().
5. Read SDMMC_CLKCR register → CLKDIV = 0 (bypass), confirmed by oscilloscope showing 100 MHz on CLK line.

### Register dump confirming the issue

SDMMC1_CLKCR:  0x00025000
  CLKDIV:      0          ← bypass, no division
  WIDBUS:      01 (4-bit)
  BUSSPEED:    0  (DS/HS)

RCC D1CCIPR SDMMCSEL: PLL2_R = 100 MHz
→ SDMMC_CK = 100 MHz (should be 50 MHz max for HS at 3.3V)

## Suggested Fix

**Option A** — Guard ConfigWideBusOperation with USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER:

Title: [Bug]: DMA DBM: transfer-complete callback dispatch appears inconsistent with callback naming, despite release note claiming a fix

Body:
### Bug Summary

DMA double-buffer mode: transfer-complete callback dispatch appears inconsistent with callback naming

### Detailed Description

In STM32H7 HAL DMA double-buffer mode (DBM), the transfer-complete callback dispatch in HAL_DMA_IRQHandler() appears inconsistent with the callback naming.

From a user's point of view, the expected meaning is straightforward:

- XferCpltCallback -> Memory0 transfer complete
- XferM1CpltCallback -> Memory1 transfer complete

This is also the natural extension of single-buffer mode, where XferCpltCallback simply means that the buffer transfer has completed.

However, the current DBM code selects the callback based on the current value of the CT bit:

metadata.issue_title: [Bug]: DMA DBM: transfer-complete callback dispatch appears inconsistent with callback naming, despite release note claiming a fix
[Bug]: DMA DBM: transfer-complete callback dispatch appears inconsistent with callback naming, despite release note claiming a fix

text:
- XferCpltCallback
- XferM1CpltCallback

If the current implementation is correct, then the documentation/comments should explicitly explain the callback meaning relative to CT and buffer switching, because the current behavior is not clear from the callback names.

I observed this behavior change after updating from STM32CubeH7 v1.12.1 to v1.13.0.

### Expected Behavior

In DMA double-buffer mode, the transfer-complete callbacks should match the buffer that has just completed:  - XferCpltCallback should be called when Memory0 transfer is complete - XferM1CpltCallback should be called when Memory1 transfer is complete  This would match the callback naming and the natural expectation from single-buffer mode.

### Actual Behavior

In DMA double-buffer mode, the transfer-complete callback dispatch appears to depend on the current CT bit value after buffer switching:  - when CT = 1 (DMA currently targets Memory1, so Memory0 has just completed), HAL calls XferM1CpltCallback - when CT = 0 (DMA currently targets Memory0, so Memory1 has just completed), HAL calls XferCpltCallback  As a result, the callback dispatch appears inverted relative to the buffer that has actually just completed.

After a successful single-shot conversion, I am unable to simply restart the DFSDM via HAL_DFSDM_FilterRegularStart_DMA. The driver state prevents a re-trigger. Currently, the only way to restart the conversion is to completely de-initialize and re-initialize the peripheral, which is not ideal.

I attempted to call HAL_DFSDM_FilterRegularStop_DMA inside the ConversionComplete callback (IRQ) to reset the state. However, this causes the driver to enter an Error State.
It appears that because the DMA transfer has already finished (due to Normal Mode), the Stop function treats the inactive DMA as an error condition.

Feedback:
In my opinion, this logic seems incorrect:
HAL_DFSDM_FilterRegularStop_DMA should not return an error simply because the DMA has already stopped naturally. It should handle this state gracefully.

There should be a standard way to re-trigger a Single Shot without forcing a full De-Init/Re-Init cycle or implementing manual workarounds to clear error flags.

Could you please verify if this behavior is intended or if there is a recommended standard procedure for this specific use case?

Best regards,

Markus

Title: AES CCM Encryption and Decryption operations output overflow

Body:
**Describe the set-up**
Custom board with STM32H730XX.

AES CCM encryption and decryption are performed with settings:

DataType = CRYP_DATATYPE_8B
DataWidthUnit  = CRYP_DATAWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
KeySize = CRYP_KEYSIZE_128B
HeaderWidthUnit = CRYP_HEADERWIDTHUNIT_BYTE

**Describe the bug**
There is an overflow in the HAL’s CRYP_AESCCM_Process when the payload length is not a multiple of 4 bytes. No masking is applied when the output block is read from the HW output FIFO, that leads to data being written beyond the output buffer.

Depending on where the buffer is and if it accounts for required alignment the overflow might lead to different consequences.

An encryption overflow example below uses the following key, nonce, ad (_they don't matter much for the issue_):

key[] = {
	0xf5, 0x95, 0x5f, 0xe1,
	0xdd, 0x84, 0x74, 0xfd,
	0x85, 0xe5, 0xfc, 0xf8,
	0x20, 0x33, 0x70, 0x01
}
nonce[] = {
	0x26, 0xd4, 0xf1, 0xfc,
	0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00,
	0x00, 0x00 ,0x00 ,0x02
}
ad[]= {
	0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00,
	0x00, 0x00 ,0x00 ,0x02,
	0x15, 0xfe, 0xfd, 0x00,
	0x02
}

Given 15 bytes payload:

metadata.issue_title: AES CCM Encryption and Decryption operations output overflow

text:
plaintext[] = {
	0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04,
	0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08,
	0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C,
	0x0D, 0x0E, 0x0F
}

it is expected to produce 15 bytes ciphertext:

expected_output[15] = {
	0xf8, 0x75, 0xe9, 0x1c,
	0xe7, 0xb5, 0xf2, 0x7c,
	0x1c, 0x54, 0x6a, 0xd9,
	0x87, 0x92, 0xca
}

in reality it produces 16 bytes where the first 15 bytes are correct (_as expected_), but an extra 16th byte - 0x3e is written:

0x24029898   xf8   0x75   0xe9   0x1c   0xe7   0xb5   0xf2   0x7c
0x240298a0   x1c   0x54   0x6a   0xd9   0x87   0x92   0xca   0x3e
0x240298a8   x00   0x00   0x00   0x00

If we reduce the plaintext to 13 bytes, then we will get  3 extra bytes.

Some libraries (_e.g. MbedTLS_) use a single shared buffer that contains both the plaintext/ciphertext and the authentication tag. Because of the overflow, the trailing bytes overwrite the tag section, resulting in tag corruption during decryption.

**How To Reproduce**
Perform AES‑CCM encryption and/or decryption with the HAL where the payload length is not a multiple of 4, and direct the result into a larger empty buffer than the payload.
The output will overflow the expected payload area and corrupt subsequent bytes.

The CRYP_AESCCM_Process should account for CRYP_DATATYPE_8B and avoid filling the output buffer as
      *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypOutBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypOutCount) = temp[index];.

# STM32 HAL DSI Read Threshold: A Likely Bug in MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE Handling

metadata.issue_title: HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly

text:
**The STM32 HAL's datasize > 2U threshold for sending MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE appears incorrect per the MIPI DSI specification.** When reading exactly 2 bytes, the HAL does not send this command, potentially causing the display peripheral to return only 1 byte. The correct condition should likely be datasize > 1U or datasize >= 2U to ensure 2-byte reads work reliably. Other vendors like Samsung/Exynos and even other STM32 HAL functions always send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE unconditionally, avoiding this edge case.

## The core issue: peripheral default behavior is undefined

The MIPI DSI specification (versions 1.0 through DSI-2) does **not mandate a universal default** for the maximum return packet size when the Set Maximum Return Packet Size command (Data Type **0x37**) is never issued. This critical detail is explicitly left as **peripheral-dependent behavior**. Most display controller ICs default to returning only **1 byte** if not instructed otherwise, as this is the most conservative assumption.

metadata.issue_title: HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly
HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly

text:
This means when datasize == 2, the command **is not sent**. If the peripheral defaults to 1 byte (as many do), it will use a 1-byte short read response (0x21) instead of a 2-byte response (0x22), returning only half the requested data. The STM32 HAL appears to assume peripherals always support 2-byte short reads without explicit configuration—an assumption the specification does not guarantee.

## Vendor implementations reveal divergent approaches

A survey of major vendor implementations shows significant variation in handling this threshold:

| Vendor/Driver | Threshold Logic | MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE Sent For |
|---------------|-----------------|------------------------------|
| **STM32 HAL** | datasize > 2 | Only reads ≥3 bytes |
| **Qualcomm MSM** | rlen <= 2 check | Only reads >2 bytes |
| **Samsung Exynos** | Unconditional | Every read operation |
| **Linux DRM core** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |
| **MediaTek** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |
| **Synopsys DW-DSI** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |

metadata.issue_title: HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly

text:
Samsung's Exynos driver takes the **most conservative approach**, always sending MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE regardless of read size. Qualcomm's MSM driver uses similar logic to STM32 but assumes short reads (≤2 bytes) work without explicit configuration. The Linux kernel core delegates this entirely to panel drivers, which must call mipi_dsi_set_maximum_return_packet_size() explicitly before reads.

## The specification's response type selection mechanism

According to MIPI DSI v1.1 Section 8.2, the peripheral follows this decision tree when responding to read commands:

1. Determine how much data the register actually contains
2. Clamp this value to MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE (if set)
3. If resulting size ≤ 2 bytes: use Short Read Response (1-byte or 2-byte variant)
4. If resulting size > 2 bytes: use Long Read Response with actual payload

When MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE is **not configured**, the peripheral uses its internal default—which the specification allows to be **as low as 1 byte**. This explains why 2-byte reads can fail: the peripheral has no indication that 2 bytes are expected and may cap its response at its default of 1 byte.

## Documented STM32 HAL DSI issues support this analysis

metadata.issue_title: HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly
HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly

text:
**Option 2: Pre-configure MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE manually**
Before calling HAL_DSI_Read() for 2-byte reads, manually send:
c
HAL_DSI_ShortWrite(&hdsi, 0, DSI_MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE, 0x02, 0x00);

**Option 3: Always send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE before every read**
Wrap HAL_DSI_Read() with a function that unconditionally sends the command first, matching the Samsung/Exynos approach.

## Technical rationale for the recommended fix

The threshold datasize > 2U is logically flawed because short read responses cover **both** 1-byte and 2-byte cases. The STM32 code **_implicitly assumes_** peripherals will automatically use 2-byte responses when 2 bytes are available, but this requires the peripheral to know 2 bytes are expected. Without MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE, a peripheral defaulting to 1 byte has no way to know a 2-byte response is acceptable.

The correct logic should be: send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE whenever the requested size exceeds the **minimum guaranteed default** of 1 byte. This means datasize > 1U or simply always sending the command. The slight protocol overhead (one additional 4-byte short packet) is negligible compared to the reliability gained.

## Conclusion

metadata.issue_title: HAL_DSI_Read not handle 2 bytes read properly

text:
The STM32 HAL DSI driver's datasize > 2U threshold represents a **latent bug** that manifests when reading exactly 2 bytes from peripherals that default to 1-byte maximum return packet sizes. While some displays may work due to having larger defaults, the implementation is not specification-compliant for the general case. Developers encountering 2-byte DSI read failures should modify the threshold to datasize > 1U or manually send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE before reads. Samsung's approach of unconditionally sending the command remains the most robust solution, adding minimal overhead while ensuring cross-peripheral compatibility.

Title: I2C Tx DMA race condition causes no Tx-complete IRQ

Body:
**Describe the set-up**
STM32H753 in custom product, compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc 14.3 rel1

**Describe the bug**

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/d649ed2c7784bfbef4be144e7bfd8dbb41dce5c3/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_i2c.c#L2055-L2076

The modification to CR1 on line 2075 races with the IRQ that is enabled on 2072.

Even though the TX DMA has not been set up, the transfer *has*. That means that the peripheral will begin the addressing phase, which may lead to a NACK interrupt.

If that NACK interrupt occurs between the read and write of the |= operation on 2075, then line 2075 ends up reverting the interrupt enable bits configured by the IRQ handler.

In practice, this means that the NACK and ERR interrupts are reenabled, and the STOP interrupt is cleared. This is then a critical failure because a NACK has already occurred, and the HAL needs to see a STOP in order to call the Tx complete callback.

In the end, this leads to a situation where the Tx complete callback is never called and you have to abort the HAL to get back to a working state.

**How To Reproduce**

text:
[george-palmsens - 2025-11-20T07:04:37Z]
> Hello [@george-palmsens](https://github.com/george-palmsens),
> 
> Thank you for the report.
> 
> Regarding your issue, could you please share more details about your project, it seems to be a particular case as you mentioned using STM32H753 in custom product and that this is heavily time dependent. Also, have you tried compiling with -O0 and -O3 optimization levels?
> 
> With regards,

Hello,

I can't share much detail, but I can explain how the calls work.

We are in a FreeRTOS environment doing the following steps:

1. The thread calls HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_DMA
2. The thread goes to sleep awaiting an event
3. The transmission finishes, either with HAL_I2C_MasterTxCpltCallback or HAL_I2C_ErrorCallback
4. The callback wakes up the thread
5. The thread proceeds to the next step.

In the failure case, step 3 never happens because the HAL gets stuck. The I2C peripheral is left in the following state:

metadata.issue_title: I2C Tx DMA race condition causes no Tx-complete IRQ

text:
- state = HAL_I2C_STATE_BUSY_TX
- mode = HAL_I2C_MODE_MASTER
- XferISR = I2C_Master_ISR_DMA
- Stop flag is set, all other flags are not
- NACK IE and ERR IE are enabled, all other interrupts are not
- DMA is enabled with TX complete IRQs enabled, but 16 bytes remaining in NDTR that aren't going anywhere

This is the root of why the HAL is stuck. The HAL _should_ be waiting for the STOP interrupt. But because of the race condition I described, the flags got reverted and it is waiting for the wrong IRQs.

---

I have not tried changing optimisation levels, this is being run at -Og.

My expectation is that the bug will exist regardless of optimisation levels (since it's a fundamental race condition), but whether you actually _see it happen_ will depend heavily on the specific timings of your project. If the clock speeds or optimisations are changed, I expect you may see the problem go away just because the timing is different. But the race condition is still there.

Title: AES GCM Invalid Tag Generation after Decryption

Body:
**Describe the bug**
An invalid tag is generated for payloads that are not a multiple of 4, as described in [Re: STM32U545 AES GCM Tag mismatch - STMicroelectronics Community](https://community.st.com/t5/stm32-mcus-security/stm32h730-aes-gcm-tag-issue/m-p/806718/highlight/true#M8519).

ST Internal ticket number: **210917**.

**How To Reproduce**
An example STM32Cube-IDE project is generated with STM32CubeMX and attached in the mentioned [community thread](https://community.st.com/t5/stm32-mcus-security/stm32h730-aes-gcm-tag-issue/m-p/807226/highlight/true#M8522).

**Describe the set-up**
Custom board with STM32H730XX.

AES GCM encryption and decryption are performed with settings:

DataType = CRYP_DATATYPE_8B
DataWidthUnit  = CRYP_DATAWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
KeySize = CRYP_KEYSIZE_128B
HeaderWidthUnit = CRYP_HEADERWIDTHUNIT_BYTE

**Additional context**

metadata.issue_title: AES GCM Invalid Tag Generation after Decryption

text:
Tag is generated correctly when:
* When the input array is 16 bytes, but we decode 15 bytes (_as there is only 15 bytes of data_).
* When we dynamically allocate an aligned input array of size that is a multiple of _4_,
   but decode with real size (_i.e, 15_).
* When the input array is in the global scope (_regardless of its size_).

The tag is generated incorrectly:
* When the input array is 15 bytes on the stack.

Tried to flush and invalidate the input memory area, as well as to flush ECC (_as buffers are located within SRAM with enabled ECC)_, no difference.

After further investigation, the culprit seems to be the padding bytes.

During the encryption, the CRYP_CR_NPBLB is used to let HW know which bytes to discard;
However, during the decryption process, it is not used/or available.

Here is the debug info, which shows that the input with 16 bytes has explicit 00 padding in the last word (0x00a989d1); whereas when the input buffer is 15 bytes, we get 8a instead of 00 in the last word (0x8aa989d1).

Working with 16 length:

When CrypInCount == 3
p/x *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypInCount)
$2 = 0xa989d1

Not working with 15 length:

gdb

0x24021c54: 0x13    0xb4    0xc7    0x2b    0x38    0x9d    0xc5    0x01

After correction of the padding in the last block (_16 bytes_) of the last writable word (_4 bytes_) the tag generation works fine after decryption, required changes are applied to CRYP_AESGCM_Process in stm32h7xx_hal_cryp.c:

I've also came along this bug, I can reproduce this.

The HAL cannot handle payloads that are not multiple of wordsize if the latest word is not padded with zeros. In this case encrpytion/decrpytion is still correct, but the generated tag is wrong.

Title: LL driver routine RCC_GetHCLKClockFreq ignores D1CPRE divider from D1CFGR register

Body:
Hello,
I'm using the STM32H743VIT6 board and arm-none-eabi-gcc compiler version 14.2.0 with -O0 option. I'm not using CubeMX setup or bigger HAL driver in this project, only LL routines mixed with some CMSIS-style register access.

It seems that LL driver routine LL_RCC_GetSystemClocksFreq() incorrectly determines HCLK frequency when non-unit D1 core prescaler (D1CPRE) is set.

metadata.issue_title: LL driver routine RCC_GetHCLKClockFreq ignores D1CPRE divider from D1CFGR register

text:
The following behavior looks like a potential bug:
1. Setup PLL1 sourced from HSE so that pll1_p_ck = 96 MHz in integer mode (lines 18-44 in my MRE below)
2. Set D1 core prescaler = 2, i.e. D1CPRE = 0b1000 in the D1CFGR register of RCC block (line 47 in MRE)
3. Set dividers for AHB, APB1...APB4 = 1 (lines 48-52 in MRE)
4. Select system clock sys_ck to be sourced from pll1_p_ck, i.e. 96 MHz (line 53 in MRE)
5. Call LL_RCC_GetSystemClocksFreq(&clk) (line 67 in MRE)
6. Now clk.SYSCLK_Frequency = 96 MHz (correct), but clk.HCLK_Frequency = 96 MHz which is incorrect since it should be HCLK = sys_ck / D1CPRE = sys_ck / 2 = 48 MHz. Consequently, all other PCLKx_Frequency are incorrect as well (96 MHz instead of 48 MHz). Also LL_RCC_GetSystemClocksFreq(&clk) does not calculate clk.CPUCLK_Frequency what looks inconsistent too.

Some debugging suggests that this routine [Src/stm32h7xx_ll_rcc.c](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/57ed86b4c358e2333a71fd895b17f1ccdb68739e/Src/stm32h7xx_ll_rcc.c#L1731) simply ignores D1CPRE as if it were always = 1. It divides SYSCLK by HPRE from D1CFGR register, but does not divide it further by D1CPRE from the same register.

Title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() can present the PTP TX timestamp of a different packet to the application code if preempted

Body:
I described several locking and concurrency problems of HAL_ETH in issue #72 #71 #70 and #69. This is another one related to the improper or missing locking via gState and HAL_ETH_STATE_BUSY.

If HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() gets preempted and another call to itself in another threads get scheduled (the functions is racing with itself), then the PTP timestamps stored in heth->TxTimestamp may be overwritten with those of another packet before the application callback HAL_ETH_TxPtpCallback() or heth->txPtpCallback() in the original call to HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() gets executed.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1437-L1467

This would cause the application code to read the overwritten PTP timestamp and not the timestamp of the packet it actually sent.

metadata.issue_title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() can present the PTP TX timestamp of a different packet to the application code if preempted

text:
This problem could be solved by either locking properly and atomically via gState or by not storing the timestamp in heth->TxTimestamp but in a stack variable in HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() and handing that stack pointer to the application which would be unique per thread.

Title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() does not test gState and races with itself and TX functions when accessing TX descriptors and counters

Body:
HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() does **NOT** check gState before execution **AT ALL**.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1400-L1413

It just runs and modifies TX descriptors, decrements buffer counters and reads state from &heth into local variables.
This buffered state can become stale/outdated if HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() gets preempted and other threads issuing calls to HAL_ETH_Transmit_IT() or HAL_ETH_Transmit() get scheduled instead.

Among other things HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() contains the decrement of dmatxdesclist->BuffersInUse.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1477

for which the increment has been guarded by a critical section

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L3333-L3340

metadata.issue_title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() does not test gState and races with itself and TX functions when accessing TX descriptors and counters

text:
So somebody suspected there might be race conditions there but failed to follow through ;)

You really, really, really need to lock this properly with atomic Test-and-Set of gState, because even the read-modify-write of TX descriptor OWN bits is potentially racy (see #71 #70 and #69)

This is not a theoretical bug! Under high incoming packet load (~8000 packets per second RX) there are frequent preemptions by the input thread which runs with realtime priority (code generated by CubeIDE).

![grafik](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f3a52b25-3eaf-4ad7-90fe-6b3d20e4e569)

This causes the TX calls and TX packet releases in other threads to be preempted and scheduled randomly and thrashes the data in &heth to a point where the system would not send TX packets any more. Under low packet load this can still occur and leads to unstable TX operation where systems will stop transmitting data after multiple days when these race conditions randomly occur but with much lower probability.

Title: HAL_ETH does non-atomic Test-and-Set operations on gState which is not thread-safe

Body:
HAL_ETH uses gState as a "poor man's mutex" to guard it's internal state and associated hardware registers against concurrent access and enforce a specific order of initialization.

When gState gets tested and set to BUSY for example, HAL_ETH does critical things to its own state or the hardware:

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L863-L866

Yet these test and set operations are not done atomically (e.g. inside a critical section) so the HAL_ETH locking via gState is vulnerable to race conditions in situations with preemption (e.g. with lwIP + FreeRTOS)

text:
To think a little more about "non-preemptive environments": Imagine a scenario without preemption (no RTOS) where the user code runs in a main-loop and sends one TX packet every second. Then you connect a button to the system that triggers an interrupt and sends a time-critical notification packet directly from the IRQ handler. You would expect this to be ok, since the packets are handed to the DMA via descriptor lists. But effectively your IRQ code is preempting the main-loop and might cause the same concurrency issues that RTOS preemption would if the calls to HAL_ETH are not thread-safe. This gets even worse with nested IRQs where even interrupts can be interrupted. So even in a bare-metal scenario with only IRQs the user would have to guard the HAL_ETH usage themselves to make it function correctly under all circumstances. So whatever performance you think you gain by omitting thread-safety cannot be gained "legitimately" because the user has to add back thread-safety in the user code.

But this is more thought experiment and colored by my opinion. I am sure you will do the right thing and sort this out in a sensible fashion and thank you for taking these bug reports seriously.

- HAL_ETH_STATE_READY means: you can register callbacks now, but to start the actual hardware and the interrupts please call HAL_ETH_Start() or HAL_ETH_Start_IT()

Custom board or nucleo,

**Describe the bug**
In HAL_ETH_ReadData(), the ptp timestamp retrieval is completely incorrect. If timestamping is enabled, is at least one descriptor is given by DMA which is the normal descriptor. Then, the next descriptor following it will be the context descriptor. The way the HAL_ETH_ReadData() function is written, it will exit as soon as it sees a normal descriptor (rxdataready will be set to 1). The next call of the function would then read the context, but one single call to this function should read both the normal packet information AND the timestamp data for that packet.

**How To Reproduce**
NA

metadata.issue_title: Ethernet PTP timestamp retrieval is entirely wrong

text:
4. How we can reproduce the problem
Enable timestamping, notice you need two calls to HAL_ETH_ReadData() to get the packet first, then the timestamp second

**Additional context**
ST needs to pay attention when writing peripheral drivers. The reason for this issue is that the MAC IP block for the Stm32F7 (and similar parts) works differently. The timestamp comes in as an extension to a normal descriptor (An "enhanced" descriptor"). This means that it's not an extra descriptor which is generated, which is *unlike* the Stm32H7's MAC IP block (which makes an additional "context" descriptor"). This is clearly a copy and paste error.  Additionally, this is evidence that ST didn't test the PTP functionality, because they would have immediately noticed this issue.

BusFault when calculating a HASH

text:
Note that the pointer cast violates the strict aliasing rule and thus invokes Undefind Behavior, but that's not the real problem here.
The actual problem is that more data is read then required in case Size is not a multiple of 4. When pInBuffer is at the end of a memory region and not 32-bit aligned, this can cause a BusFault.
For example, when the buffer is located at the end of the AXI SRAM on the STM32H753, reading one byte too much will cause the MCU to read from Reserved memory and thus cause a BusFault.

The following example code should demonstrate this:

c
uint8_t pOutBuffer[32];

uint8_t *pInBuffer = (uint8_t *)0x2407FFD1; // 47 bytes before the end of AXI SRAM
uint32_t Size = 45; // 45 bytes (so the input buffer is still completely inside AXI SRAM)

HASH_Start(&hhash, pInBuffer, Size, pOutBuffer, HAL_MAX_DELAY, HASH_ALGOSELECTION_SHA256); // will crash

A solution would be to handle the last 1-3 bytes (in case Size is not a multiple of 4) separately, thereby avoiding reading out-of-bounds.

Title: Incorrect assertion in HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel() for STM32H7

Body:
**Description of the set-up**
* STM32H753
* CubeMX 6.6.1
* STM32H7 HAL v1.11.0

**Description of the bug**

The function HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel() contains the following check:
c
  /* if ROVSE is set, the value of the OFFSETy_EN bit in ADCx_OFRy register is
     ignored (considered as reset) */
  assert_param(!((sConfig->OffsetNumber != ADC_OFFSET_NONE) && (hadc->Init.OversamplingMode == ENABLE)));

I guess the assertion is (incorrectly) copied from the STM32L4 (or other device) HAL code, for which this check is correct. The STM32L4+ reference manual (RM0432 Rev 9) states the following, which matches the description in the code comment:
> Offset correction is not supported in oversampling mode. When ROVSE and/or JOVSE bit isset, the value of the OFFSETy_EN bit in ADC_OFRy register is ignored (considered as reset).

However, according to the reference manual (RM0433 Rev 7):
> The offset correction is also supported in oversampling mode.

metadata.issue_title: Incorrect assertion in HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel() for STM32H7

text:
Since the offset correction is also supported in oversampling mode on the STM32H753, this assertion is incorrect and should be removed or modified (OffsetRightShift and OffsetSignedSaturation are not supported in oversampling mode, so probably those should be checked instead).

**How To Reproduce**

Call HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel() with sConfig->OffsetNumber defined to another value then ADC_OFFSET_NONE (e.g. ADC_OFFSET_1) and hadc->Init.OversamplingMode set to ENABLE and USE_FULL_ASSERT defined.

However, the calibration factor is 11 bits, so I think the check should be <= 0x7FFU.

/**

Title: DMA2D_IRQHandler called with empty ISR register

Body:
I'm using a custom board with STM32H723 (144pin), 5inch display (LTDC), external SRAM (FMC), external NOR flash (OSPI) with Touchgfx and DMA2D (double buffer strategy). No OS.

I experimented **random stucks of the touchgfx** like described in [this](https://community.st.com/s/question/0D53W00000e067WSAQ/ui-stuck-in-takeframebuffersemaphore) thread. After struggling I found out that the problem was caused by **DMA2D_IRQHandler called with empty ISR register**. In fact, the touchgfx was expecting a call to _XferErrorCallback(hdma2d)_ that never happened and so hanged on.

For what I've seen when this _empty call_ is triggered the _DMA2D_FLAG_TC_ should be HIGH, but actually this sometimes doesn't happens.

I do not know why this happens (silicon bug? touchgfx clean the flag in particular moment?), but for sure the HAL library doesn't manage this case.

So to solve my issue I changed in void HAL_DMA2D_IRQHandler(DMA2D_HandleTypeDef *hdma2d){...} of _stm32h7xx_hal_dma2d.c_ the following line:
if ((isrflags & DMA2D_FLAG_TC) != 0U)
in
if ((isrflags & DMA2D_FLAG_TC) != 0U || isrflags == 0U)

Title: Missing ReceiveToIdle API in HAL USART

Body:
There doesn't seem to be a ReceiveToIdle API for the USART devices while there is one for UART devices. This is an issue when, in my case for board layout reasons, switching from UART to USART. The peripheral does support it, it's just missing in HAL.

Comments:
[ASELSTM - 2022-04-08T14:23:56Z]
Hi @sdekrijger,

First, thank you for your contribution. The objective of the ReceiveToIdle APIs is to allow application to handle use cases where number of data to be received is unknown. It is useful for the UART case as communication is asynchronous, the Transmitter and Receiver don't share a clock reference. Therefore, unless a start bit detected, the receiver does not know exactly when it will receive a data.

For USART case this can be driven by the CLK synchronization signal. As long as there is data to be received as long as there is signal on the CLK pin. Once no more activity is detected on the clock line, thus reception is over. As per referenced in the reference manual :

metadata.issue_title: Missing ReceiveToIdle API in HAL USART

text:
> In master mode, the SCLK pin operates in conjunction with the TX pin. Thus, the clock is provided only if the transmitter is enabled (TE=1) and data are being transmitted (USART_TDR data register written).

The clock signal can then provide an overview of the data transfer status, even if the amount of data to be received is unknown.

Hence, we do not have plans to add ReceiveToIdle APIs for the USART driver.  Please allow me then to close this issue. Thank you for your comprehension and thank you once again for your contribution.

text:
The legacy include legacy/stm32_hal_legacy.h is always brought into the build by stm32h7xx_hal_def.h.
stm32h7xx_hal_def.h is #included  by some of the modules (e.g. stm32h7xx_hal_rcc.h).

Those "HAL_DBGMCU_*" definitions only exist in the HAL on those lines in legacy/stm32_hal_legacy.h.

In my case this causes issues with automated unit test mock function generation using Ceedling, as it generates a mock function called HAL_DBGMCU_EnableDBGSleepMode() instead of the expected HAL_EnableDBGSleepMode().

The file stm32h7xx_hal_def.h should probably not #include legacy/stm32_hal_legacy.h.

Title: Ethernet: Add ability to explicitly free specific descriptors or release descriptor with new address

Body:
In embedded IP stack usage (e.g. lwip), which is typically implemented as zero-copy, the presently available interfaces for recycling RxDescriptors is problematic. Ideally, when a packet is received and read out of the HAL, the driver code would pass this buffer to the stack, and would only release the descriptor back to the HAL driver when the stack releases this buffer (e.g. through a pbuf_free() call).  Between pushing this message into the stack, and the stack _freeing_ this buffer back to the driver (and thus the descriptor to the HAL), it's possible that additional packets are received that go through this same process.

Given the scenario above, in a multi-threaded environment, there is no way to guarantee the order the packets are _freed_ is the same order in which they are _received_. The only support approach in the HAL driver is to free all consumed RX descriptors through the HAL_ETH_BuildRxDescriptors() call, but as the freeing may happen in a different order, this approach may cause descriptors to get re-used before the data has been consumed.

metadata.issue_title: Ethernet: Add ability to explicitly free specific descriptors or release descriptor with new address

text:
Ideally, the user would be able to release RX descriptors in any order and as singalled by the stack through pbuf_free() like calls.  A few possible ideas for this would be...

1. Simplest API would be to release the last descriptor (single), but with a new buffer address, for example HAL_ETH_ReleaseOneRxDescriptor(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, void *new_buffer_address). This could optionally be extended to take an array or even something like an ETH_BufferTypeDef linked list, HAL_ETH_ReleaseRxDescriptors(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, ETH_BufferTypeDef *buffers) although implementing this from the user code with multiple calls to ReleaseOne might actually be a little more straightforward than creating the linked list.

1. API such as HAL_ETH_ReleaseRxDescriptor(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, uint32_t index).  For this API to work, the user would need to be able to also get the descriptor indices associated with the  for HAL_ETH_GetRxDataBuffer() possibly it could be embedded in the ETH_BufferTypeDef or through a separate HAL_ETH_GetRxDescriptorInfo() such that it could then be tracked and freed when available.

Title: HAL_FDCAN_GetRxMessage() evaluates GetIndex value for Rx FIFO overwrite scenario.

Body:
Dear HAL Driver developer,

STM32H753 Reference Manual informs below:

When an Rx FIFO is operated in overwrite mode and an Rx FIFO full condition is signaled, reading of the Rx FIFO elements should start at least at get index + 1. The reason for that is that it can happen that a received message is written to the message RAM (put index) while the CPU is reading from the message RAM (get index). In this case inconsistent data may be read from the respective Rx FIFO element. Adding an offset to the get index when reading from the Rx FIFO avoids this problem.

However the below code which evaluates the GetIndex and then the Read RxAddress does not seem to test for Overrun condition. As per above information I understand that code need to be modified to first check for overrun condition is needed. Then in case of overrun condition the GetIndex should be incremented by 1 (based on rollover condition) and then used for calculating RxAddress:
